summary: OAuth access tokens are often bearer tokens, meaning anyone who steals one can use it. DPoP (Demonstrating Proof of Possession) has the client prove at the application level that it holds a particular key each time it uses a token. This makes stolen access and refresh tokens much harder to replay.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally an OAuth access token is a ticket: whoever holds it can use it. DPoP changes that by making the token useless without a matching key. The client signs every request with that key, so a thief who copies the token still has nothing to sign with.

questions: how to prevent oauth token replay
how does dpop prevent token theft
subtitle: How an OAuth client proves, on every request, that it holds the private key a token was issued to, so stolen tokens are not enough.

tldr.problem: Typical bearer tokens can be used by anyone who holds them, so a leaked or stolen access or refresh token can be replayed by an attacker.
tldr.mechanism: The client signs a small JWT, the DPoP proof, with its own private key and sends it in a DPoP header on each request. The authorization server binds tokens to the matching public key, and servers check the proof against that key.
tldr.outcome: A stolen token alone becomes unusable without the private key, though DPoP does not stop an attacker who can run code inside the client or replace the TLS layer.

today: RFC 9449 is a Proposed Standard, published in September 2023. No RFC obsoletes it and no RFC updates it.

sections.title: Binding a Token to a Key
sections.content:
Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) is an application-level mechanism for sender-constraining OAuth (RFC 6749) access and refresh tokens. It enables a client to prove the possession of a public and private key pair by including a DPoP header in an HTTP request. The value of the header is a JSON Web Token (RFC 7519) that enables the authorization server to bind issued tokens to the public part of a client's key pair. Recipients of such tokens are then able to verify the binding of the token to the key pair that the client has demonstrated it holds via the DPoP header. In other words, the legitimate presenter of the token is constrained to be the sender that holds and proves possession of the private part of the key pair.

The mechanism can be used where other methods of sender-constraining tokens that use elements of the underlying secure transport layer, such as RFC 8705 or OAuth 2.0 Token Binding, are not available or desirable. Due to a poor user experience of TLS client authentication in user agents and a lack of support for HTTP token binding, neither mechanism can be used if the OAuth client is an application that is dynamically downloaded and executed in a web browser, sometimes called a single-page application. Applications that are installed and run directly on a user's device are also well positioned to benefit from DPoP-bound tokens that guard against the misuse of tokens by a compromised or malicious resource, because such applications often have dedicated protected storage for cryptographic keys.

DPoP can be used to sender-constrain access tokens regardless of the client authentication method employed, but DPoP itself is not used for client authentication. It can also be used to sender-constrain refresh tokens issued to public clients, those without authentication credentials associated with the client ID.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is simple: the token is tied to a key, and the key stays with the client. The token travels; the key does not. This works in a browser, where asking the browser to hold a client certificate is awkward, and it works for a native app, which usually has a secure place to keep a private key.

sections.title: Why Bearer Tokens Are a Problem
sections.content:
The primary aim of DPoP is to prevent unauthorized or illegitimate parties from using leaked or stolen access tokens, by binding a token to a public key upon issuance and requiring that the client proves possession of the corresponding private key when using the token. This constrains the legitimate sender of the token to only the party with access to the private key, and gives the server receiving the token added assurances that the sender is legitimately authorized to use it.

Access tokens that are sender-constrained via DPoP stand in contrast to the typical bearer token, which can be used by any party in possession of such a token. Although protections generally exist to prevent unintended disclosure of bearer tokens, unforeseen vectors for leakage have occurred through vulnerabilities and implementation issues in other layers of the protocol or software stack, such as the CRIME and BREACH compression attacks, Heartbleed and the Cloudflare parser bug. There have also been numerous published token theft attacks on OAuth implementations themselves. DPoP provides a general defence in depth against the impact of unanticipated token leakage. It is not, however, a substitute for a secure transport, and MUST always be used in conjunction with HTTPS.

The typical OAuth interaction necessarily makes the client disclose the access token to the protected resources it accesses. The attacker model in the security topics document describes cases where a protected resource might be counterfeit, malicious or compromised, and plays received tokens against other protected resources to gain unauthorized access. Audience-restricted access tokens, using the JWT aud claim, can prevent such misuse, but doing so in practice has proven to be prohibitively cumbersome for many deployments, despite extensions such as RFC 8707. Sender-constraining access tokens is a more robust and straightforward mechanism to prevent such token replay at a different endpoint, and DPoP is an accessible application-layer means of doing so.

Because of the potential for cross-site scripting, browser-based OAuth clients bring added considerations for protecting tokens. The most straightforward XSS attack is for an attacker to exfiltrate a token and use it themselves, completely independent of the legitimate client. A stolen access token is used for protected resource access, and a stolen refresh token is used for obtaining new access tokens. If the private key is non-extractable, as is possible with the Web Crypto API, DPoP renders exfiltrated tokens alone unusable.

XSS vulnerabilities also let an attacker execute code in the context of the browser-based client application and maliciously use a token indirectly through the client. That execution context has access to the signing key, so it can produce DPoP proofs to use with the token. At this application layer there is most likely no feasible defence against that threat except generally preventing XSS, so it is considered out of scope for DPoP.
sections.plainLanguage: Tokens leak. They leak through compression tricks, through parser bugs, and through attacks on the server that issues them. Restricting a token to one audience helps but is awkward to deploy. Tying the token to a key is a stronger rule that does not depend on every other layer being perfect.

sections.title: The DPoP Proof JWT
sections.content:
DPoP introduces the concept of a DPoP proof, a JWT created by the client and sent with an HTTP request using the DPoP header field. Each HTTP request requires a unique DPoP proof. A valid proof demonstrates to the server that the client holds the private key that was used to sign it, which lets authorization servers bind issued tokens to the corresponding public key and lets resource servers verify the binding of the tokens they receive.

The DPoP proof is a JWT signed with JSON Web Signature (RFC 7515) using a private key chosen by the client. The JOSE header MUST contain at least three parameters. The typ field has the value dpop+jwt, which explicitly types the proof as a DPoP proof JWT. The alg field is an identifier for a JWS asymmetric digital signature algorithm, and it MUST NOT be none or an identifier for a symmetric algorithm. The jwk field represents the public key in JSON Web Key format and MUST NOT contain a private key.

The payload MUST contain at least four claims. The jti is a unique identifier for the proof; its value MUST be assigned so that there is a negligible probability the same value is assigned to any other proof used in the same context during the window of validity, which can be accomplished by encoding at least 96 bits of pseudorandom data or by using a version 4 UUID string. The htm claim is the HTTP method of the request the JWT is attached to, and the htu claim is the HTTP target URI of that request, without query and fragment parts. The iat claim is the creation timestamp of the JWT.

When the proof accompanies an access token at a protected resource, it MUST also contain the ath claim, the hash of the access token: the base64url encoding of the SHA-256 hash of the ASCII encoding of the token's value. When the server provides a DPoP-Nonce header, the proof MUST also contain a nonce claim with that recent value. A proof MAY contain other header parameters or claims defined by extension, profile or deployment-specific requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The proof is a small signed token that says which request it belongs to. It names the HTTP method and the address, carries a timestamp and a random identifier, and includes the hash of the access token so the proof cannot be reused with a different token.

sections.title: Checking a DPoP Proof
sections.content:
To validate a DPoP proof, the receiving server MUST ensure that there is not more than one DPoP HTTP request header field; that the header field value is a single and well-formed JWT; that all required claims are present; that the typ header parameter has the value dpop+jwt; that the alg parameter indicates a registered asymmetric digital signature algorithm, is not none, is supported by the application and is acceptable per local policy; that the JWT signature verifies with the public key in the jwk header parameter; and that the jwk parameter does not contain a private key.

The server must also check that the htm claim matches the HTTP method of the current request, and that the htu claim matches the HTTP URI value for the request in which the JWT was received, ignoring any query and fragment parts. If the server provided a nonce value, the nonce claim must match it. The creation time of the JWT, as determined by either the iat claim or a server managed timestamp via the nonce claim, must be within an acceptable window. Finally, if the proof is presented to a protected resource together with an access token, the server must ensure that the ath claim equals the hash of that access token and confirm that the public key to which the access token is bound matches the public key from the DPoP proof.

To reduce the likelihood of false negatives, servers SHOULD employ syntax-based normalization and scheme-based normalization before comparing the htu claim. These checks may be performed in any order.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks the signature, checks that the proof is for this request and this token, checks that it is fresh, and checks that the key in the proof is the key the token was issued to. All of that has to pass before access is granted.

sections.title: Binding the Token to the Key
sections.content:
Resource servers MUST be able to reliably identify whether an access token is DPoP-bound, and to obtain enough information to verify the binding to the public key of the DPoP proof. The binding is accomplished by associating the public key with the token in a way that the protected resource can access, such as embedding the JWK hash in the issued access token directly, using the syntax described in this section, or through token introspection. Other methods are possible by agreement between the authorization server and the protected resource, but they are beyond the scope of the specification. Resource servers supporting DPoP MUST ensure that the public key from the DPoP proof matches the one bound to the access token.

When access tokens are represented as JWTs, the public key information is represented using the jkt confirmation method member. To convey the hash of a public key in a JWT, the specification introduces a JWT Confirmation Method (RFC 7800) member for use under the cnf claim. The value of the jkt member MUST be the base64url encoding of the JWK SHA-256 Thumbprint, according to RFC 7638, of the DPoP public key in JWK format to which the access token is bound.

To request an access token that is bound to a public key using DPoP, the client MUST provide a valid DPoP proof JWT in a DPoP header when making an access token request to the token endpoint. This applies to all access token requests regardless of grant type. The DPoP header field MUST contain a valid DPoP proof JWT, and if the proof is invalid the authorization server issues an error response with invalid_dpop_proof as the value of the error parameter. To sender-constrain the token after checking the proof, the authorization server associates the issued access token with the public key from the proof. A token_type of DPoP MUST be included in the access token response to signal that the token was bound to its DPoP key.
sections.plainLanguage: The token records a fingerprint of the public key, so any server that receives the token can tell which key it belongs to. The token type in the response says the token is bound; if the response says Bearer, the token is not bound and the client should decide whether that matters.

sections.title: Using a DPoP-Bound Token at a Resource
sections.content:
A DPoP-bound access token is sent using the Authorization request header field with an authentication scheme of DPoP. The syntax of the Authorization header field for the DPoP scheme uses the token68 syntax for credentials, so the credentials are the string DPoP followed by one or more spaces and the token value.

For such an access token, a resource server MUST check that a DPoP proof was also received in the DPoP header field of the HTTP request, check the DPoP proof according to the rules in Section 4.3, and check that the public key of the DPoP proof matches the public key to which the access token is bound. The resource server MUST NOT grant access to the resource unless all checks are successful.

Refresh tokens issued to confidential clients are not bound to the DPoP proof public key, because they are already sender-constrained by a different existing mechanism. OAuth 2.0 already requires the authorization server to bind refresh tokens to the client to which they were issued, and requires confidential clients to authenticate when presenting one, so such refresh tokens are sender-constrained by way of the client identifier. That existing mechanism is more flexible, for example allowing credential rotation without invalidating refresh tokens, than binding directly to a particular public key. When an authorization server supporting DPoP issues a refresh token to a public client that presents a valid DPoP proof at the token endpoint, the refresh token MUST be bound to the respective public key, and that binding MUST be validated when the refresh token is later presented to get new access tokens.
sections.plainLanguage: At the resource server, the token is presented with the DPoP scheme instead of Bearer, and the proof travels alongside it. The server compares the key in the proof with the key the token was bound to. A mismatch means the request is refused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations cover several separate issues. DPoP proof replay is addressed by the requirement that each HTTP request carries a unique proof, with a unique jti value and a creation timestamp that a server can check against an acceptable window. A server that supplies a nonce can also require that the proof carries it, which tightens the window further.

DPoP proof pre-generation is a concern for scripts running in the browser. Malicious code can create proofs with timestamps in the future and exfiltrate them with a token, so servers can optionally require clients to include a server-chosen value in the proof that an attacker cannot predict. Without that optional nonce, the impact of pre-computed proofs is limited by the proof being bound to an access token on protected resource access: because a proof covering an access token that does not yet exist cannot feasibly be created, access tokens obtained with an exfiltrated refresh token and pre-computed proofs will be unusable.

A DPoP nonce downgrade is possible if a server issues a nonce and a client does not use it, so a server that provides a nonce MUST require it in subsequent proofs. Untrusted code in the client context is, as the objectives section says, out of scope, because such code can reach the signing key.

Signed JWT swapping is addressed by requiring the htm and htu claims, so a proof captured from one request cannot be replayed against another. Signature algorithms are restricted to registered asymmetric algorithms, and neither none nor a symmetric algorithm is acceptable.

Request integrity is partial: only the HTTP method and URI are covered by the proof, so the request body is not protected by it. Access token and public key binding is protected by the ath claim and the jkt binding, and authorization code and public key binding is achieved with the dpop_jkt authorization request parameter, whose value is the JWK Thumbprint of the proof-of-possession public key using SHA-256, the same value used for the jkt confirmation method. When a token request is received, the authorization server computes the JWK Thumbprint of the public key in the DPoP proof and verifies that it matches the dpop_jkt parameter value in the authorization request; if they do not match, it MUST reject the request. Use of the parameter is OPTIONAL, and it may be combined with PKCE, which is recommended as a countermeasure to authorization code injection.

Hash algorithm agility and binding to client identity are also discussed, and the specification notes that DPoP is not a substitute for a secure transport.
sections.plainLanguage: Each proof is single-use, carries a fresh random identifier and a timestamp, and names the exact request it belongs to. The server can additionally hand out a nonce, which makes it much harder to prepare proofs in advance. What the proof does not cover is the request body.

items.title: typ
items.text: dpop+jwt, so the proof cannot be mistaken for another kind of JWT.

items.title: alg
items.text: A registered asymmetric signature algorithm; never none and never a MAC.

items.title: jwk
items.text: The client's public key, with no private key in it.

items.title: jti
items.text: A unique identifier, at least 96 bits of random data.

items.title: htm and htu
items.text: The HTTP method and target URI the proof is for.

items.title: iat
items.text: The creation timestamp, checked against an acceptable window.

items.title: ath
items.text: The hash of the access token, present when a token accompanies the proof.

items.title: nonce
items.text: A server-chosen value, when the server provides one.
